brief.t: Started in 1978 in Chennai as the Murugappa Group's finance company, first financing equipment; vehicle loans are now its biggest business.
Vehicle finance is about half the loan book (₹1,29,787 cr in Sep 2026); the rest is loans against property, home loans, SME, consumer and gold loans.
FY 2025-26: consolidated profit ₹5,233 crore (+23%) and AUM ₹2,42,630 crore (+21%).
Q2 FY27 (Jul–Sep 2026): profit ₹1,630 crore (+41%), AUM ₹2.68 lakh crore (+25%); the board approved raising up to ₹5,000 crore through a QIP.
Leaders: Vellayan Subbiah, Executive Chairman since 1 Apr 2025; Ravindra Kumar Kundu, Managing Director since 7 Oct 2024.

timeline.t: Incorporated in Chennai as the Murugappa Group's financial services company, starting with equipment financing.
Long-time executive Ravindra Kumar Kundu became Managing Director (five-year term).
Named by the RBI in its list of Upper Layer NBFCs for 2024-25.
Vellayan Subbiah became Executive Chairman for five years (to 31 Mar 2030).
Entered gold loans; 308 dedicated gold loan branches by Sep 2026.
AUM crossed ₹2.68 lakh crore; board approved a QIP of up to ₹5,000 crore.

model.how: Chola borrows money from banks, bond markets and other lenders, and lends it on to customers, mostly in smaller towns. Its biggest business is loans for new and used commercial vehicles, cars, tractors and two-wheelers. It also gives loans against property, home loans, SME and consumer loans, and now gold loans. It earns the gap between the interest it charges and its cost of funds.
flow: Borrow from banks, bonds and NCDs
Lend: vehicle, property, home, SME, gold loans

points: Chola is an Upper Layer NBFC, so the RBI applies stricter, bank-like rules to it.
Vehicle loans depend on truck, car and tractor sales; management expects demand to support growth across vehicle types.
NBFCs must keep capital adequacy of at least 15%; Chola was at 20.62% in Sep 2026.

glossary.NBFC: Non-Banking Financial Company: a lender regulated by the RBI that gives loans but cannot take savings or current account deposits like a bank.
glossary.AUM: Assets Under Management: the total loans an NBFC has given out and not yet been repaid. The main size measure for a lender.
glossary.Disbursements: New loans paid out to customers in a period.
glossary.Net profit: What is left after all costs, provisions and taxes. The company's final earnings.
glossary.Net Interest Income: Interest earned on loans minus interest paid on borrowings. A lender's main earning.
glossary.Net interest margin: Net Interest Income as a % of loans or interest-earning assets. Shows how profitable lending is.
glossary.Gross NPA: Loans not repaid for 90+ days (called 'Stage 3' loans by NBFCs), as a % of all loans.
glossary.Net NPA: Bad loans after subtracting the money already set aside (provisions) for them. Lower is better.
glossary.Stage 3 assets: Loans that have stopped paying for 90+ days. NBFCs report Gross and Net Stage 3, similar to banks' NPA.
glossary.Credit cost: Money set aside for bad loans, as a % of average loans. Lower means fewer losses.
glossary.Capital adequacy ratio: The lender's own capital compared with the risk in its loans. RBI requires NBFCs to keep at least 15%.
glossary.Provisions: Money set aside from profit to cover loans that may not be repaid.
glossary.Borrowings: Money an NBFC raises from banks, bonds (NCDs), commercial paper and, for some, public deposits, to lend onward.
glossary.Cost of funds: The average interest an NBFC pays on its borrowings. NBFCs usually pay more than banks, so a strong credit rating matters.
glossary.Credit rating: An agency's grade (e.g. AAA) of how safely a company can repay debt. Higher ratings mean cheaper borrowing.
glossary.Upper Layer NBFC: The largest and most important NBFCs, named by the RBI under its scale-based rules. They face bank-like rules and must list on the stock market within 3 years.
glossary.Return on assets: Net profit as a % of average total assets. Shows how well a lender earns on what it owns.
glossary.Dividend: Part of the profit paid to shareholders, per share.
glossary.Attrition: The % of employees who leave in a year. Also called employee turnover.
glossary.RBI: Reserve Bank of India, which regulates banks and NBFCs in India.
glossary.KYC: Know Your Customer: checking a customer's identity before giving a loan.
glossary.MSME: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises: small businesses that lenders serve.
glossary.Cross-sell: Selling an extra product (like insurance or a second loan) to an existing customer.
glossary.Co-lending: A bank and an NBFC lending together: the NBFC finds and services the borrower, the bank funds most of the loan.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first sells its shares to the public.
glossary.BRSR: Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report: an official yearly report on people, environment and governance that big listed companies must publish.
glossary.Vehicle finance: Loans to buy trucks, buses, cars, tractors, two-wheelers and construction equipment. The vehicle is the security for the loan.
glossary.Loan against property: A loan given against a house or shop the borrower owns, often used by small business owners.
glossary.Gold loan: A short-term loan given against gold jewellery kept with the lender.
glossary.QIP: Qualified Institutions Placement: a quick way for a listed company to raise money by selling shares to large institutional investors.
glossary.Return on equity: Net profit as a % of shareholders' money. Shows how well the company uses its owners' capital.

Finance.q: Chola's profit grew 41% but AUM grew 25%. Why the gap?
Finance.a: Net income rose 24% while loan losses fell 3% year on year, so more of the income reached profit.

Finance.q: What is the difference between Gross Stage 3 (3.25%) and GNPA under RBI norms (4.44%)?
Finance.a: Stage 3 is based on 90+ days overdue under Ind AS. RBI norms classify more loans as NPA (for example, a loan stays NPA until all dues are cleared), so the RBI figure is higher.

Finance.q: Why would Chola raise ₹5,000 crore through a QIP?
Finance.a: Fast loan growth uses up capital; fresh equity keeps capital adequacy well above the 15% minimum and supports future growth.

Marketing.q: How would you grow Chola's gold loan business?
Marketing.a: Use existing vehicle-loan customers and branch towns, offer quick disbursal and safe storage, and promote through local campaigns in the South and East.

Marketing.q: How can Chola win more used-vehicle loan customers?
Marketing.a: Tie up with used-vehicle dealers and brokers, offer fast approvals through the app, and cross-sell insurance.

HR.q: Chola hires many field staff in small towns. How would you reduce early attrition?
HR.a: Hire locally, give clear training and career paths, recognise collection and sales wins, and support managers to coach new joiners.

Sales.q: Sell a used-truck loan to a small transport operator.
Sales.a: Ask about routes and income, show the EMI against monthly earnings, explain quick approval and local branch support, then agree on documents and next steps.

Operations.q: How would you improve collections in a rural vehicle-loan branch?
Operations.a: Track early overdue accounts daily, understand seasonal farm and freight incomes, offer digital payment options and visit borrowers early.

Other.q: What do you know about Chola?
Other.a: A Chennai-based Murugappa Group NBFC from 1978, led by Executive Chairman Vellayan Subbiah and MD Ravindra Kumar Kundu; vehicle loans are about half of its ₹2.68 lakh crore AUM.

interview.why_us: Chola has grown from an equipment finance company in Chennai into a lender with ₹2.68 lakh crore of loans, most of them in small-town India. It is backed by the Murugappa Group, is growing in new areas like gold loans, and gives young people early responsibility in sales, credit and collections. I want to contribute to [your role] and learn how lending works on the ground.
ask: How will the gold loan business fit with the vehicle finance branches?
What will the QIP money be used for over the next two years?
What does success look like for a new joiner in the first six months?

gd.t: Should NBFCs face the same rules as banks?
gd.for: Large NBFCs like Chola lend as much as mid-sized banks, so similar rules protect the system.
gd.against: NBFCs serve small-town borrowers that banks miss; heavy rules can slow that lending.

gd.t: Are gold loans good for India?
gd.for: Quick, secured credit for families and small businesses without much paperwork.
gd.against: Borrowers can lose family jewellery if they cannot repay, and gold prices can swing.

avoid: Don't call Chola a bank; it is an NBFC regulated by the RBI and cannot take savings deposits.
Don't confuse Cholamandalam Investment and Finance (the lender) with Cholamandalam Financial Holdings (its holding company) or Chola MS General Insurance.
Don't quote the Feb 2026 media report on the Chairman's exit as fact; the company denied it.
